questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Etre as a verb of identity
questions.learningObjective: identify the work etre does in a sentence that assigns a role
questions.stem: A woman fills in a staff card and writes « Je suis infirmière depuis cinq ans ». What is etre doing in the opening clause?

options.text: assigning her a role that the sentence says she still holds
saying she owns a uniform and works only at night
options.misconception: reads etre as a verb of ownership, which is avoir's work

options.text: reporting that she reached the hospital five years ago
options.misconception: hears a present tense and gives it the job of the passe compose

options.text: placing her inside a building for a limited stretch of time
options.misconception: assumes etre can express location on its own, which it cannot

questions.explanation: Etre states what somebody is, and an occupation belongs to the layer of a life that lasts, so it takes etre. The five years come from « depuis », not from the verb. The tempting moves are all borrowings from elsewhere: avoir covers ownership, the passe compose covers one dated event, and location in French needs etre followed by a place word, as in « Elle est à l'hôpital », never etre alone. A speaker who hears « elle est l'hôpital » hears a mistake, not a variant.

it classifies the studio as one particular kind of dwelling

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Avoir with age and sensation
questions.learningObjective: show why a passing condition cannot be given to etre
questions.stem: A nurse writes on a chart: « Vous avez de la fièvre depuis deux jours. » Why can that sentence not be built with etre?

options.text: because a fever is a condition that comes and goes, not a lasting identity
because etre cannot stand in front of an indefinite article
options.misconception: believes etre is barred by un or une, which is false

options.text: because the partitive article selects avoir as its verb
options.misconception: thinks de la chooses the verb rather than following it

options.text: because depuis can only appear beside a form of avoir
options.misconception: ties the choice of verb to the preposition that follows it

questions.explanation: French splits being and having across two verbs, and a fever belongs to the having side, so « vous avez de la fièvre » is right. What changes from one day to the next is not what a person is. The traps here are all surface rules that do not exist: etre works perfectly well with an article, as in « Elle est une pianiste », and « depuis » decides nothing, since « Elle est ici depuis midi » is ordinary. The partitive article belongs to the noun, not to the verb in front of it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the fever will still be part of who the patient is next month.

the first reports possession; the second assigns a class

options.misconception: reduces the two verbs to a single function

options.text: the first stands in the present; the second is a past form
options.misconception: reads avoir in the present as though it were a dated past

Behind both sits one rule: etre marks what somebody is and where they are, avoir marks what they have. The tempting reading hears the à and reaches for a preposition of possession, as English does with at, and hears an avoir in the present and assumes a past. French makes neither of those moves.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Etre and avoir side by side
questions.learningObjective: teach one test that separates etre from avoir
questions.stem: A learner asks you for a single test that separates etre from avoir, and hands you three sentences they are unsure about. Explain the test and show it working on all three.

answer.exemplar: The test is the question hiding behind the verb. Ask « est-il ? » about the subject; if the sentence answers that, the verb is etre, and if it answers « a-t-il ? », the verb is avoir. « Je suis étudiant » answers what he is, so etre. « J'ai un vélo » answers what he has, so avoir. « Elle est en retard » answers where she is, so etre. The test settles the awkward cases too: « Ils ont faim » describes nothing about what they are, and « Il a dix ans » reports a fact that will change, not an identity.

questions.explanation: French splits being and having across two verbs, and what decides the choice is the question the sentence answers about its subject, not the kind of noun that follows. That is why the same subject can carry both in one breath: « Elle est étudiante et elle a dix-huit ans » states a class and then an age, and each verb is doing the job it is there for. The commonest learner error is to choose by the noun rather than by the question, which produces « elle a étudiante » and « elle est dix-huit ans »; a speaker hears those as a change of meaning, not a slip of the pen.
questions.hint: Ask what question the sentence is really asking about its subject.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Accent on the infinitive as a spelling decision
questions.learningObjective: explain why the accent on the infinitive settles the stem vowel
questions.stem: A learner asks why acheter sometimes becomes achète while peser never becomes pète, and wants the rule that decides it rather than a list of exceptions. Explain the difference.

answer.exemplar: The mark on the infinitive already announces the sound, so it decides what the verb may do later. In peser the é is written precisely to say the vowel stays closed, so no change of stem is possible: je pèse, nous pesons, vous pesez. In acheter the infinitive ends in er with a plain e, which may open in front of an ending that is itself an e, so the singular forms show è, j'achète, and the nous and vous forms close back to e, nous achetons, vous achetez. The same split appears in presented, je présente but nous présentons. So the rule is about what the spelling has already settled, and the infinitives in -é and -ès are simply verbs where the spelling has settled everything.

questions.explanation: The accent is not decoration on the infinitive; it is a promise about the vowel that every later form keeps. A verb written with é or è has a fixed vowel and cannot dip anywhere, so peser,payer and lever stay open or closed for good, while a verb written with a plain e in -er has a choice and takes it in front of the endings in e. This is why a learner who learns the change as a rule about j'achète and then applies it to peser is reading a spelling as though it were a sound.
questions.hint: Ask what the accent on the infinitive has already told you about the vowel.

The two rejected lines fail for opposite reasons: one spreads a singular-only change across the plural, and the other moves a vowel that the spelling has already fixed.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Si with the imperfect and the conditional
questions.learningObjective: explain the tense pairing a conditional condition requires
questions.stem: A learner writes « Si j'avais le temps, je viendrai » and asks why the past tense cannot stay in the second clause. Explain the pattern the language uses and what it conveys.

answer.exemplar: A condition that the speaker treats as unlikely or imaginary is put in the imperfect, and its consequence goes in the conditional, so the sentence is « Si j'avais le temps, je viendrais ». The imperfect marks the condition as belonging to a stretch the speaker cannot point to, and the conditional reports the result that would follow inside that stretch. A condition the speaker treats as real keeps both clauses in the present: « Si je suis en retard, j'appelle. » The temptation is to keep one tense across both clauses, and a learner who does produces « Si j'avais le temps, je viendrai », which sounds as though the visit were still expected.

questions.explanation: French marks the difference between a real and an imagined condition in the tenses themselves, and the pairing is fixed: imperfect for the condition, conditional for the consequence. The speaker is not reporting that a past condition was true but placing the whole statement inside a possibility, which is why the mood of both verbs softens. questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The pronoun en
questions.learningObjective: identify what en stands in for
questions.stem: Stage one: say exactly what the two partitive phrases in « Elle a mangé du pain et du fromage » contribute. Stage two: rewrite the sentence so that one pronoun carries both of them at once.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the two partitive phrases say that some bread and some cheese were eaten without saying how much, and they keep the verbs own meaning intact, since a manger takes two objects quite comfortably. Stage two: Elle en a mangé, where en stands for du pain et du fromage, and en is the one pronoun that can gather a phrase with several nouns behind a single verb. The order matters: en comes before the auxiliary because it belongs to the verb, so « elle en a mangé » and never « elle a en mangé ». A learner who leaves one of the nouns behind has written a sentence about a single foodstuff, which is a different claim.

That is what lets it gather two nouns behind one verb in a single pronoun, and the two uses are the reason so many idioms in French are built on it. The placement rule is the same as for every other pronoun: in front of the verb, and in front of the auxiliary when there is one.
questions.hint: Ask which single pronoun can stand in for both nouns at once.

questions.topic: The four relative pronouns
questions.learningObjective: match a relative clause to the pronoun it needs

qui for the report, because que never stands for a thing
options.misconception: believes qui is reserved for people and cannot reach an object

options.misconception: reaches for a preposition phrase where a plain object is meant

options.text: où for the report, because it points at the nearest possible referent

questions.topic: A demonstrative or a possessive
questions.learningObjective: tell ce from son by the test of a replacement phrase
questions.stem: A colleague says « son livre est prêt » while another says « ce livre est prêt ». How can a listener tell which book is meant?

the two sentences are identical in meaning and differ only in length
options.misconception: believes a determiner choice carries no information at all

options.misconception: reads a possessive as though it were a category

options.misconception: confuses the two halves of the demonstrative system

questions.topic: Adjective position and a change of meaning
questions.learningObjective: explain why a shift of position can change what an adjective says

the first is spoken and the second is only ever written down

questions.topic: Joining two clauses with car and donc
questions.learningObjective: tell a reason connector from a consequence connector
questions.stem: A writer joins two clauses and writes « Il a plu toute la journée, donc les jardins sont secs. » What does the connector tell the reader?

the second clause is offered as the cause of the first

options.text: the writer is quoting somebody else rather than speaking

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Four connective roles in one paragraph
questions.learningObjective: assign a connective to each of the four jobs in a paragraph
questions.stem: A writer wants to join sentences so a reader can follow the reasoning: a reason, a result, a concession and a new start. Explain what each of car, donc, pourtant and néanmoins contributes and where each can sit.

answer.exemplar: Each of the four points in one direction, and confusing them is what makes a paragraph unreadable. Car states a reason and joins it to a claim inside the sentence, so it normally takes no comma: « Il pleut, car nous n'avons rien prévu ». Donc states a result, and it works either after the verb, « Il pleut, donc nous sommes restés à la maison », or at the start of the sentence, « Donc nous sommes restés à la maison ». Pourtant and néanmoins both state a concession, and the difference between them is one of position rather than meaning: nevertheless is common at the head of a sentence, « nevertheless we went », in careful prose, while pourtant is more at home inside the clause, « nous y sommes allés pourtant ». Aucune des trois n'affaiblit la phrase; elles indiquent seulement la logique.

questions.explanation: A connective is a promise about the relationship between two clauses, and a reader who has been promised one and given another has to stop and work out what was meant. Car is a reason and stays inside the sentence, donc is a result and can open a sentence, and the two words for concession, pourtant and néanmoins, carry the same logic in slightly different habits of position. The temptation is to treat them as interchangeable links in a chain, which is exactly how a paragraph loses the thread the writer thought it had.
questions.hint: Ask which direction each connector points in, and whether it can open a sentence.

questions.topic: Four ways of asking the same question
questions.learningObjective: reject a question that stacks a tag on top of est-ce que
questions.stem: A classmate writes the same question four times: « Est-ce que tu es prêt ? », « Tu es prêt ? », « Es-tu prêt ? » and « Est-ce que tu es prêt, n'est-ce pas ? ». Which one needs rewriting?

the third, because inversion is barred with a pronoun subject
options.misconception: believes inversion has been closed to tu after the interrogative word

options.text: the second, because a question may not be made by word order alone
options.misconception: forgets the way French turns a statement into a question

options.text: the first, because est-ce que requires an inversion behind it
options.misconception: adds an inversion the construction does not ask for

questions.explanation: French has three ways of asking, and any one of them will do the job. Est-ce que can stand in front of any subject, inversion is available with tu, il, elle and on, and a tag turns a statement into a question, as in « Tu es prêt, n'est-ce pas ? ». What the language will not do is stack them, so « Est-ce que tu es prêt, n'est-ce pas ? » asks twice over and a speaker hears it as clumsy rather than polite. A learner who has learned one of the three can use it everywhere.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sentence already contains two separate ways of making a question.
